name: DuckLake
summary: A lakehouse format that keeps table metadata in an ordinary SQL database and the data in Parquet files.
intro: Iceberg and Delta Lake keep a table’s metadata as files next to the data: manifests, snapshots and logs that every reader has to fetch and stitch together. DuckLake moves all of that into a SQL database instead. The catalog (which files belong to which table, every snapshot, the schema history) lives in PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL or a DuckDB file. The data itself stays as plain Parquet files on S3, another object store, or local disk.

A commit is one database transaction, so changes across several tables can be atomic, and finding the files for a query is one SQL lookup instead of a chain of object-store reads. Small writes can be held in the catalog database first (“data inlining”) and flushed to Parquet later, which avoids the small-files problem. DuckDB has first-class support through its `ducklake` extension, and DuckLake 1.0 shipped in April 2026 with a backward-compatibility guarantee.
strengths: No catalog server to run: any database you already operate, such as PostgreSQL, is the catalog
Snapshots, time travel, schema evolution and multi-table ACID transactions
Data is ordinary Parquet, so it isn’t locked in; you can copy tables out to Iceberg
Fast small commits, because metadata updates are database rows rather than new files
limits: DuckDB’s `ducklake` extension is the reference implementation; other engines, such as DataFusion, are only starting to add support
The catalog database sets the limit: if it’s slow or down, so is every table in the lake
A DuckDB-file catalog allows only one client; use PostgreSQL for many readers and writers
Younger than Iceberg and Delta Lake, with a smaller ecosystem of tools

story: Iceberg and Delta Lake made tables on object storage practical, but they keep their metadata as files. Iceberg uses what DuckLake’s authors called “a maze of JSON and Avro files” to record schemas, snapshots and which Parquet files belong to a table. Every small change writes more metadata files, and reading a table means a chain of sequential HTTP requests before the first byte of data. To find the current version safely, both formats also ended up adding a catalog service, which is itself backed by a database.

On 27 May 2025, Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen of the DuckDB project proposed DuckLake: if a database is needed anyway, put all the metadata in it and keep only the data in Parquet. They pointed out that Google BigQuery (with Spanner) and Snowflake (with FoundationDB) already manage metadata this way, “just without the open formats at the bottom.” The spec stores catalog, snapshots and statistics as ordinary tables in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite or DuckDB.

Version 0.3 added Iceberg interoperability in September 2025, and DuckLake 1.0 shipped on 13 April 2026 with a stable spec and a backward-compatibility guarantee. Engines beyond DuckDB have started to follow, such as an Apache DataFusion integration in July 2026.

choices.choice: Metadata in a SQL database, data in Parquet
choices.why: The authors’ view is that blob storage is great for scaling data files, but tracking snapshots, schemas and statistics is a job for a database, as BigQuery and Snowflake already do internally.

choices.choice: A commit is one database transaction
choices.why: Iceberg and Delta Lake essentially manage one table at a time. Using the database’s own transactions gives atomic changes across many tables for free.

choices.choice: Small changes can be inlined into the catalog
choices.why: Small writes are the lake’s worst case: each one adds files to compact later. DuckLake can keep small inserts as rows in the metadata database, which allows sub-millisecond writes.

choices.choice: Any ACID SQL database can be the catalog
choices.why: There is no catalog server to deploy: a DuckDB file works on a laptop, and PostgreSQL works for many readers and writers.
